author: Freedom Editor
title: Court halts sanctions against Autistici/Inventati
content:
Italian tech collective was de-banked following “terrorism” designation by the Trump regime

An important ruling against financial overreach: United States anti-terrorism lists do not have automatic legal effect in Italy. The judge has ordered the immediate unblocking of an account, reaffirming the limits on the power of banks.

This significant decision extends well beyond the specific case of Autistici/Inventati, establishing a concrete limit on the United States’ attempt to extend its own sanctions globally. In an order dated 20 November, the Court of Pisa granted an urgent appeal filed by the association Autistici/Inventati (AI ODV) against Banca Popolare Etica, ordering the immediate restoration of full access to the association’s current account and the funds held within it. The bank was also ordered to pay the legal costs.

The ruling, signed by Judge Teresa Guerrieri, addresses a situation that began on August 26, when the U.S. Department of the Treasury—through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)—placed Autistici/Inventati on a list of entities subject to anti-terrorism sanctions. A few days later, on 1 September, Banca Etica informed the association of a “temporary limitation on account operations,” effectively rendering the funds in the account inaccessible. The bank justified this action by citing the need to assess the client’s updated risk profile and the potential implications of the American sanctions.

The Court of Pisa rejected this position, establishing a fundamental principle: inclusion on an OFAC list does not automatically trigger an obligation to freeze funds under the Italian legal system. Any asset-freezing measures must be grounded in national or European Union law, rather than merely in the decision of a foreign administrative authority. An American designation may be a factor to consider in risk assessment and anti-money laundering (AML) due diligence obligations; however, it does not authorise a bank to render a client’s entire account inaccessible—on a general basis and for an indefinite period.

This point is particularly significant because the judge draws a clear distinction between the monitoring obligations of financial intermediaries and the power to impose actual restrictive measures. While AML regulations allow for enhanced due diligence and, in certain circumstances, the refusal to execute specific transactions, they do not grant banks an independent, broad-reaching power to freeze assets. In the case of A/I, Banca Etica failed to identify any binding Italian or European legal instrument—or any contractual provision—that could justify a total block on the client’s funds.

Even more relevant is the reasoning regarding so-called “secondary sanctions,” through which Washington exerts pressure on non-U.S. economic entities. The court acknowledges that U.S. sanctions can have tangible economic consequences for European intermediaries, but clarifies that this risk does not equate to an automatic recognition of their legal validity within the Italian legal system. Citing the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, the judge underscores the necessity of distinguishing between the economic impact of extraterritorial measures and their legal legitimacy in Europe.

This is precisely the political crux of the matter that we have highlighted since the beginning of this case. The power of US sanctions lies not merely in the measures adopted in Washington, but in their capacity to influence the decisions of banks, platforms, and service providers in other countries. The fear of economic repercussions drives these intermediaries to act as enforcers of foreign decisions, even in the absence of any domestic legal obligation requiring them to do so. The result is a form of economic repression in which exclusion from essential services can precede any judicial determination.

The Court of Pisa addresses this very mechanism, asserting that banking prudence cannot devolve into an arbitrary power to suspend contractual rights. The ruling further acknowledges the disproportionate nature of the freeze: rendering the association’s only account inaccessible effectively prevented it from fulfilling its obligations and carrying out its normal activities—all without any specific justification being provided for opting for a blanket restriction rather than scrutinising individual transactions.

Naturally, this court order does not overturn the OFAC designation, nor does it constitute a judgement on the overall legitimacy of the accusations levelled by the Trump administration against Autistici/Inventati. Its scope is more specific, yet no less significant: an administrative decision made in the United States cannot be automatically transformed by an Italian bank into an asset-freezing measure that lacks an adequate legal basis.

Following the shutdown announced by A/I last September, this ruling represents a significant validation of the arguments put forward by the collective and its legal counsel. While it does not undo the harm caused by U.S. sanctions, nor does it resolve the issue of European digital and financial infrastructure’s dependence on the United States, it does demonstrate that Washington’s attempt to impose its anti-terrorism lists globally can face concrete legal limitations.

The case of Autistici/Inventati thus remains an emblematic example of how dissent is criminalised through economic and administrative measures. However, the Court of Pisa’s decision establishes a non-negotiable principle: the fear of U.S. sanctions cannot take precedence over Italian law, and banks cannot arrogate to themselves the power to freeze assets—a power not granted to them by the legal system.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Silicon Valley’s blueprint for autocracy
content:
For years, tech oligarchs have been converting their corporate absolutism into political leverage

Examine the current global transition from liberal-democratic societies toward autocratic, state-capitalist models, and a clear pattern emerges. Alongside a renewed greed for scarce natural resources sits a concerted drive to secure control over emerging technologies. Among key figures in the tech industry—including Elon Musk, Alexander Karp, and Peter Thiel—a conviction has taken root that CEOs would make far more suitable ruling elites than elected officials. While they currently rely on autocratic political frameworks as a foundation, their ultimate ambition is to govern states just as they run corporations.

Nobody illustrates this convergence of monopoly power and political ambition better than Peter Thiel. Having played a pivotal role in steering J. D. Vance toward the American Vice Presidency, Thiel exerts profound influence on both sides of the Atlantic through his company, Palantir Technologies, and his private networks.

The intellectual blueprint for both Thiel and Vance comes from the “neo-reactionary” theorist Curtis Yarvin, who operates the platform Urbit with Thiel’s financial backing. Yarvin openly advocates for the abolition of democracy, dismissing it as inefficient, corrupt, and incapable of solving long-term problems. In its place, he envisions a modern monarchy led by CEO-sovereigns. To justify this centralised, unilateral authority, Yarvin frequently cites historical precedents: Julius Caesar and Augustus, Napoleon as a “start-up monarch,” Franklin D. Roosevelt overseeing the Manhattan Project, and Abraham Lincoln raising troops and censoring the press without congressional consent.

Thiel’s corporate philosophy mirrors this political theory. Born in Frankfurt in 1967 and raised in California and apartheid-era South Africa, Thiel studied philosophy and law at Stanford before co-founding PayPal with Elon Musk, launching Palantir in 2003, and establishing the venture firm Founders Fund. In his book Zero to One, co-authored with Blake Masters, Thiel argues that competition and capitalism are fundamentally incompatible. True success requires building a monopoly through radical technological innovation, allowing a company to dictate pricing and plan in decades. Like Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, Thiel insulates Palantir from shareholder accountability through super-voting shares, ensuring the founder remains a kind of monopolistic monarch even when institutional giants like BlackRock hold vast stock blocks.

After mentoring J. D. Vance at Yale Law School, hiring him at Mithril Capital, and funding his firm Narya Capital, Thiel invested $10 million into Vance’s successful 2022 Ohio Senate bid—alongside fellow “PayPal Mafia” alum David O. Sacks—and backed Blake Masters in Arizona. Although Democratic candidates ultimately won both Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections, Thiel’s deepest influence lies within the executive branch.

Following Donald Trump’s election victory, Thiel’s network embedded itself directly into the federal apparatus. His former Palantir chief of staff, Michael Kratsios, became head of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. Longtime Palantir veterans Gregory Barbaccia and Clark Minor assumed top federal Chief Information Officer roles, while Michael Obadal moved from Anduril Industries—an AI defence contractor chaired by Thiel’s close associate Trae Stephens and backed by Founders Fund—to become Assistant Secretary of the Army.

This revolving door blurs the boundary between private tech monopolies and state security. Palantir’s software platforms, such as Gotham, aggregate massive datasets to guide decision-making across defence, intelligence, finance, and pharmaceuticals—often reinforcing pre-existing forms of discrimination embedded in historical data. Meanwhile, Anduril supplies the military with autonomous drones, underwater systems, and border surveillance via its AI-driven “Lattice” platform. As Palantir increasingly explores military applications—from voice-recognition monitoring and drone reconnaissance to AI partnerships with firms like Anthropic to assess operational probabilities—the tools of warfare and surveillance are consolidating under a handful of unaccountable executives.

Beyond public politics, Thiel operates a secretive economic policy circle founded in 2006 with entrepreneur Auren Hoffman. Exposed in June 2026 by the Swiss hacker “maia arson crimew,” this invitation-only “dialogue network” brings together elite figures from politics, business, and the military across European retreats. At its August 2026 gathering in Dublin, 222 members convened to discuss “dealing with a Third World War,” “technologies for the battlefield,” “establishing one’s own cults,” and “reactivating nuclear power.”

Dismissing these gatherings as mere “prepper” fantasies ignores the calibre of the attendees. Alongside Hoffman—whose companies SafeGraph and LiveRamp amass trillions of monthly consumer location and behavioural data points—the network includes U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Senator Ted Cruz, and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, whose software is utilised by ICE and the US Department of Defense.

When the same closed circle of billionaires controls mass data surveillance, autonomous weaponry, venture capital, and key government appointments, the State is no longer even a nominal democracy, but an institution shaped completely for the benefit of a self-appointed elite.

title: Microscopic mutual aid
content:
From the deepest root to the highest leaf and every acorn, bacteria and fungi cooperate with each other and their host to survive

1.8 billion years ago the mitochondria, “the powerhouse of the cell,” moved within a host cell for protection. Neither side was exploited, and equilibrium was achieved. To this day, DNA is segregated between the mitochondria and the nucleus reminding us of cellular cooperation.

In her work, On the Origin of Mitosing Cells (1967), Lynn Margulis posited that structures such as the mitochondria originated from smaller specialised cells taking refuge within larger cells. 60 years after Kropotkin, Margulis’ Endosymbiotic Theory challenged the expectations of Darwinian evolution and was rejected by 15 journals. Endosymbiosis is now a respected cornerstone of evolutionary biology.

Our cells and ecosystems exemplify cooperation, not competition. Mutual aid is the biochemical basis of multicellular life meeting required energy demands; the mitochondria was a volunteer, but now it is part of the cooperative powerhouse of the cell(s).

I research microbiomes of terrestrial plants, using advanced molecular techniques to untangle form and function in microscopic communities.

Mutual aid has been the foundation of my research. From the deepest root to the highest leaf and every acorn, bacteria and fungi cooperate with each other and their host to survive, ward off disease, and improve overall wellbeing. If natural selection is the play, molecular mutual aid is the stage, the lights, the assistant, the director, and the crowd.

Microbiomes are complex systems that include beneficial, neutral or pathogenic individuals. As scientific knowledge expands, we are beginning to understand that the difference between a beneficial and detrimental microbe could be triggered by environmental stress. The shift is not governed by a central mechanism, but by a quorum of functionally cooperative bacteria following a unifying imperative: “common survival at all costs”.

Capitalism is fundamentally Darwinian: proliferate or perish, outcompete your rivals, grow exponentially. However, bacteria have shown us that natural selection is not exponential, and neither should be our methods of measuring economic progress.

The Escherichia coli (E. coli) Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) is the clearest demonstration of natural selection to date. Founded by Richard Lenski of Michigan State University in 1988, LTEE has observed the equivalent of more than 2,000,000 years of human evolution over 75,000 generations taking advantage of the rapid rate of replication in E. coli. Every day 1% fractions of the previous community are transferred into fresh medium; each day represents more than six generations.

Using molecular techniques, the group was able to track the rate of evolution within their E. coli lineages. They predicted that rate of evolution would be hyperbolic: a period of exponential development followed by a plateau, an upper ceiling. However, it was discovered that there is no upper ceiling. Exponential improvement in E. coli fitness is succeeded by incremental developments. Adaptations become exponentially rarer but never cease.

Put simply, evolutionary adaptations become less dramatic, the return on investment diminishes as the E. coli was already adapted to a cosy temperature of 37°C for the equivalent of 2,000,000 human years.

On our own, human scale, we have seen epochs of exponential growth, such as the industrial or agricultural revolutions, where outputs were tangible and material. Accelerationists wish you to believe that the incessant integration of the latest greatest technology – currently AI – will usher in a new revolution despite diminishing returns. But we are already at the point of diminishing returns. Why are data centres becoming larger instead of smaller and more efficient? Why is my chocolate bar shrinking? Culturally, how much did music change between 1960-90, compared to between 1990-2020?

I have seen in my own data that pathogenic fungi are often present and quantifiable up to 25% of community composition, but no signs of disease are present. Certainly, there are outright pathogens that cause disease. But if you placed them in a hermetically sealed box with their host, their long-term existence is not feasible. They infect, they multiply, the host dies, their population dies after consuming all the resources.

Exponential growth of a singular microbe is the hallmark of disease, and we understand that environmental stress exacerbates symptoms. Similarly, GDP is an exponential metric placed above ecosystems, climate, and quality of life. Quantifying the stressors that push GDP beyond capital accumulation may provide an opening for the preservation of natural systems.

It is now popular knowledge that eating a healthy diet contributes to a thriving and functional “gut microbiome” which directly assists digestion. But few people are aware of how they run on the principles of mutual aid on a cellular level.

Understanding these communities, which have persisted throughout evolution, could provide a mathematical basis for economic deceleration and degrowth.

title: Trans remembrance & everyday resistance
content:
The transphobes may have won their draconian legislation, but they have lost the culture war

In July 2017, the Tory Government announced a public consultation on legal gender recognition in the United Kingdom. It aimed to bring in a system based on statutory declaration, and like many European countries, allow trans persons to obtain a Gender Recognition Certificate on the basis of a statutory declaration. This proposed change was supported by the Labour opposition and was not seen as significantly controversial.

Almost immediately, we witnessed a systematic attack on trans children, starting with claims about protecting them from untested medical inteventions and the outright lie that children under 18 were undergoing surgery. In an important case funded by American anti-abortionists, it was argued that young people aged 15 were too young to fully appreciate the consequence of taking puberty blockers. When the lower court ruled that children under 18 should not be able to receive any medical intervention, The Guardian celebrated this in its editorial as a return to common sense.

The Appeals Court judges ruled it was legal nonsense, undermined Gillick competency, and if it upheld could undermine access to contraception for women under 16 (which is why the anti-abortion brigade funded it in the first place). But by now, rebranded ‘gender criticals’ were up in arms and the damage was done to our community. The transphobes were given new life and more foundations to persecute the Tavistock Clinic for Young People and attacking youth services and schools.

Then came the billionaire author J.K Rowldemort, who got involved and began tweeting transphobia to her millions of followers and funding transphobic hate groups. Then came legal intervention by the now Labour (Blue State) government. For Women Scotland, Sex Matters and the LGB Alliance worked as a mesh to split Trans people off from LGB. Freed from the ideological shackles of Sheila Jeffries radical feminist talking points, these new transphobes could move on to fear mongering and hate not seen since the heady days of the persecution of Martina Navratilova in tennis (herself sadly now a terf)

But these culture-war attacks would have gone nowhere without the State. From Boris Johnson to Rishi Sunak to Keir Starmer, a series of deeply transphobic prime ministers have followed complete with transphobic health secretaries, education ministers and home secretaries. One minister made it illegal for teachers to refer to children in school by their preferred name. An employment tribunal agreed that gender critical employees could legally misgender their colleagues at work. Two health secretaries, one from each party, banned all prescription of hormone replacement therapy and puberty blockers for under 18s. One of them (Wes Streeting) had previously worked for leading LGBTIA campaign group Stonewall and appeared on television to defend trans women as women.

So here we are, today on this Trans Day of Remembrance: a new ‘left wing’ Labour prime minister with a gay defence secretary, a Muslim woman home secretary, a Jewish foreign secretary—honestly it sounds like an American Democrat’s fantasy—yet this government will continue to enable and apply a draconian set of transphobic policies that amount to wholesale segregation and apartheid.

Adult trans people cannot use the toilets or changing rooms of their gender identity. They will be housed in prison wards, youth offender wings, immigration hostels and hospital wards of their birth sex. They will be searched by police officers, prison officers and immigration officer on their birth sex/ In Wales, all sex replacement surgery has been cancelled despite people waiting for a decade on waiting lists.

Yet resistance persists. I don’t know a single trans person who uses the toilets of their birth sex. And there has yet to be a single reported incident of a venue or organisation forcing someone to leave. The transphobes may won their legislation, but they have lost the culture war they started. Most people see us as just women, men and nonbinary people who are surviving, just like them, in a toxic authoritarian country ruled by death eaters and bigots.

Personally, I’ve not had one woman in the toilets offer me anything other than acceptance. In those small moments when a woman tells me my dress looks nice in a public toilet, I feel a sense of recognition and solidarity. That gives me hope that out of our remembrance of past possibilities we find the strength and joy to survive and to win.

title: To remember Durruti: “Solidarity is the best incentive”
content:
Ninety years since the death of Buenaventura Durruti, the greatest military leader of the Spanish Revolution

Born into the working class on 14 July 1896 in Leon, Buenaventura Durruti became a mechanic by trade and a prominent local union organiser of the socialist Unión General de Trabajadores (UGT, General Union of Workers). Expelled from UGT after the August 1917 general strike for his militancy, he left Leon and joined the mass anarcho-syndicalist union, the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT, National Confederation of Labour), and became an anarchist. He soon became a leading activist within the movement, playing a key role in the resistance to Franco’s coup of July 1936 and the subsequent social revolution.

The Trotskyist Felix Morrow proclaimed in his Revolution and Counter-Revolution in Spain that Durruti was “the greatest military figure produced by the war” while, of course, dismissing anarchism by suggesting he was “no theoretician, but an activist leader of masses… his words express the revolutionary outlook of the class-conscious workers”. This ignores that Durruti’s words, activity, and outlook did not spring out of thin air but rather were informed by and reflected his anarchist politics, history, activity, and vision—which in turn reflected his experiences and needs as a member of the CNT and the working class.

While undoubtedly remembered as a man of action, indeed his exploits across Spain, Europe and South America are legendary, Durruti read anarchist literature and press, took part in the debates within the Spanish anarchist movement, and was a noted public speaker. However, it is for his role in the Spanish Revolution and Civil War that he is best remembered.

When the military did revolt on 17 July 1936, Durruti took a leading part in organising the resistance in Barcelona amongst the various CNT unions and defence committees. A general strike was called, weapons seized, and 19 July saw the army defeated by the people armed.

The long desired social revolution swept the city and other parts of free Spain – as anarchists had long argued, workers seized the workplaces, peasants the land, popular assemblies and revolutionary committees were formed. The collectivised economy benefited all rather than the owning class, while also providing weaponry to the militias (with workplaces refashioned to do so). Non-economic social relationships likewise began to transform, and anarchist women organised the Mujeres Libres to empower women and fight the sexism that permeated Spanish society and, sadly, the anarchist movement.

Anarchist theory, which had always argued that a social revolution could only be defended by the people armed, was also applied when the CNT organised militias to liberate those areas of Spain under military control. Other unions and parties did likewise, although unlike those the CNT militias were run by their members with elected officers and committees, all sharing the same living conditions. As Durruti argued:

“I don’t believe – and everything happening around us confirms this – that you can run a workers’ militia according to classic military rules. I believe that discipline, co-ordination, and planning are indispensable, but we shouldn’t define them in terms taken from the world that we’re destroying. We have to build on new foundations. My comrades and I are convinced that solidarity is the best incentive for arousing an individual’s sense of responsibility and a willingness to accept discipline as an act of self-discipline.”

As the Durruti column marched towards Zaragoza, liberated villages and towns started the process of transforming society and the economy by forming collectives. These voluntary groups turned the land, machinery and other resources into common property, to be managed, worked, and benefited from by all rather than a few landlords or capitalists. For Durruti, the war and the revolution were inseparable:

“Our comrades on the front know for whom and for what they fight. They feel themselves revolutionaries and they fight, not in defence of more or less promised new laws, but for the conquest of the world, of the factories, the workshops, the means of transportation, their bread and the new culture.”

With the Republican government preferring to arm the rearguard (against the revolution) over the CNT militias, the Aragon Front stagnated. Yet the CNT militias were recognised as being the best fighters, as shown by part of the Durruti being sent to Madrid to help in its defence. Whilst there, he was killed at the front line on 20 November 1936. His funeral in Barcelona saw hundreds of thousands crowd the streets to commemorate the man who embodied the libertarian social revolution and the aspirations of millions for a better world.

This cannot be anything but a summary of both Durruti’s life and the libertarian social revolution he helped create. For more details, Abel Paz’s Durruti in the Spanish Revolution cannot be bettered.

title: Why anarchists like James Bond
content:
With all our criticism of the franchise’s nationalism and misogyny, we can still enjoy the films and their flawed hero

Yesterday’s article in Freedom caused a stir on publication. When I read it I was determined to write a counter, but in doing so I have to ask myself: why on earth do I enjoy James Bond films?

Some of A. J. Boyer’s criticisms of Bond are sound, so I’m going to try to start with areas where we might find agreement. I should also say that the content of this article includes incidents in the books and films that are offensive. I mention them here to explain in more detail why liking Bond can be more than just problematic.

Around 20 years ago I decided to read Ian Fleming’s original Bond novels. I was shocked by the levels of sexism and racism in the books. On a recent re-read of Live and Let Die the use of the N word and the casual racism through his descriptions of people left me feeling sick. As consumers of culture, we don’t leave our ability to think critically on the shelf when we take the book down to read. We can read something and decide its merits and / or its lack of such. This applies to watching films too. That particular book is disgraceful. You can’t really say it’s just a product of its time. It’s the product of a man who is showing off his racism. A few years ago, elements of Fleming’s work were altered to remove some of the worst offending material. Bizarrely, the alterations didn’t include changing Bond’s reference to having sex with a particular woman as always containing the ‘sweet tang of rape’ and referring to homosexuality as a ‘stubborn disability’. There’s still much to hate about his writing despite the updating and there’s no defence for it.

I won’t include a list of all the disgusting moments in his writing but the levels of it go far beyond what occurs in the films. In the film version of Goldfinger, Bond forces himself on the ludicrously named Pussy Galore. Fleming’s book goes further and describes her as a lesbian. By the end of both the book and the film, Bond and Galore are an item. In the book, Bond has convinced her that her sexuality was an error on her part, so masculine and amazing is he.

Fleming does everyone a disservice in The Spy Who Loved Me by presenting the entire story from a female gaze; something he really isn’t equipped to do. Presented in first person, through the eyes of the character, Vivienne Michel, the novel includes her being confronted by two mobsters who break into her motel with the intention of robbing her and sexually assaulting her. Bond comes to the rescue and she enters a sexual relationship with him. Fleming includes Vivienne explaining how she rejected the brutality of the mobsters but likes the brutality of Bond. It’s another difficult read among many.

So, there’s an awful lot of reasons to dislike James Bond. Not just the character but the original novels in general. The character may be flawed but that shouldn’t mean the novels have to be. But they are. Fleming made them like that and if you tried to remove all the terrible content, some of the novels simply wouldn’t exist.

However, Andrew makes a point that I fundamentally disagree with. He states that “the James Bond franchise presents a character that is so antithetical to anarchist values, that it becomes impossible to take seriously”. Here’s the thing, though: I don’t take the films seriously. I take them as a bit of entertainment. The films are fun, silly and adventurous. The character is utterly ridiculous and horrible. He stands against everything I agree with. But Bond exists in a strange world. It is a fantastical world in many ways. It’s a world closer to science fiction than reality. The laser beam heading to Sean Connery’s crotch in Goldfinger, the invisible car in Die Another Day, Pierce Brosnan using a parachute to surf a tsunami in the Arctic without a jacket of any sort; the list of nonsense in these films is massive.

We should also note that, as the franchise has been going for over 60 years, it also provides an interesting lens to societal views throughout time. The insistence that Timothy Dalton’s Bond only stick to one sexual relationship in 1987’s The Living Daylights is the franchise’s direct response to concerns around HIV and AIDS. In more recent films, Bond is constantly criticised for his behaviour by his superiors. He doesn’t change much, but attitudes around him do. He is a much better flawed hero in the films than in the books, because the books themselves are so flawed.

Fleming could actually write well, which is all the more damning. In action scenes, his use of very short sentences encourages the reader to dart through the action. His descriptive powers are often dense as he shows off his own extensive knowledge of the world. It would be wrong to say that he couldn’t write. It’s just that he wrote some utterly appalling stuff. I don’t want to make a cheap point about Proudhon here but we’ve got some writers like this in our own canon. Interestingly, Fleming didn’t like the violence of the films, in particular the way Bond seems to relish killing people. Prior to the films he wrote From a View to a Kill, which sees the character agonise over being a sniper. It focuses on the process of going from getting that view of the intended victim through a telescopic lens, to then actually pulling the trigger. As the theme song to the film version of Casino Royal puts it, “when you take a life, do you know what you give?” When From a View to a Kill was chosen as inspiration for a film version in 1985, the word ‘from’ was omitted from the title and the subject matter changed. It is a rare moment where Fleming’s Bond is relatable, in a way.

I’m not here to defend Bond as a character and I’m certainly not here to defend Ian Fleming. I’m here to answer the argument that we can’t simply dismiss Bond as entertainment. I agree, we can’t. But we also can’t assume that every anarchist dislikes (or ought to dislike) Bond. We can’t assume that anarchists who do enjoy Bond films are simply consuming this stuff without thinking. As someone who started watching the films from a very young age—prior to the invention of ITV 2—they were a rare treat. We would go to school the next day and whatever had been shown would be the talk of the playground. I grew up with it. I grew up recognising the character was unpleasant.

There isn’t even a quantum of solace for the patriots who believe in Bond’s view of the world, as Briain’s influence fades around them. But I grew up enjoying the adventure, the wonderful music, the sci-fi gadgets, the locations I’ll probably never get to see in person. Those are the reasons I’m excited to see the next James Bond film. I’ll be keeping my critical thinking with me when I watch it.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Why anarchists hate James Bond
content:
Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007 at a time of global unrest and distaste for government

It’s been announced that Robert Pattinson has been chosen to play the next James Bond. This has come after years of speculation as to who would follow Daniel Craig. The Bond franchise in particular pins itself to a very specific time and era of Cold War espionage and patriotic spy games. Whilst we’re certainly not rid of nuclear tensions and geopolitical posturing, the general public’s attitude towards the government has changed enough to leave me wondering – what sort of person are Bond films made for?

Plenty of pragmatic anarchists are able to maintain their values whilst leisurely enjoying a pop culture franchise with morals that run counter to it. If we weren’t able to do this, we’d never get through a basic board game like chess. Star Wars, for instance, fits rather easily with our values – we can see a cautionary tale of a neoliberal society slipping into fascism in the prequels. We can then root for the revolutionaries that combat it in the original trilogy. Star Trek has a similar shared territory, with themes of communistic living (albeit still hierarchical). But the James Bond franchise presents a character that is so antithetical to anarchist values, that it becomes impossible to take seriously.

Firstly, there’s the propaganda aspect. Ian Fleming wrote ‘Casino Royale’ (the first James Bond book) back in 1953; four years after the establishment of NATO. Since then, much of the franchise features the usual tropes of damsels in distress, orientalism and an external nation that threatens (so-called) freedom and democracy. Each film was released throughout the Cold War, up until Pierce Brosnan became the first post-Soviet Bond. How entertaining the films are is neither here nor there; but the themes and stakes in which it requires the viewer to be invested act quite purposely to normalise militarism and neoliberal assumptions.

Full disclosure: I can’t honestly say I’ve seen more than one James Bond film. My friend sat me down when I was a teenager and showed me ‘Die Another Day’. At the time, I found it rather cringe to see Bond rescue a damsel in distress only to travel to a beach and make-out. Perhaps I generalise too much, but I can’t imagine being in the mood right after narrowly escaping death. My friend insisted otherwise and swore it was realistic. I can’t remember much else of the film, apart from being accused of being needlessly critical.

But certain media deserves the pushback; particularly one as backwards as James Bond. Not only from an anarchist viewpoint, but even from a Feminist one: I’ve hardly come across a woman who enthusiastically recommends I watch the likes of Sean Connery (who in an interview with Barbara Walters advocated hitting women if they “can’t leave it alone”). Nor have I known any that have been excited to see yet another actress play an objectified Bond girl.

Randolph Bourne famously stated that “war is the health of the state”; that they are one in the same. The Bond franchise mirrors the exact trajectory of people’s view towards government: problematic, and constantly requiring updates and rebrands. Without the latent external threat of some enemy government, I’m unsure what there would truly be to root for with regards to Bond. His story very much depends on the assumption that the government, bureaucracy and the military have our best interests at heart. Anarchists have long known for centuries that this isn’t the case for neither radicals nor everyday working people.

One of the nearest USA examples that comes to mind (there are many) would be the fictional agent Jack Bauer (played by Kiefer Sutherland) in the post-9/11 series 24. The series took place largely during the War on Terror and depicted torture and surveillance as a necessary evils in order to stop terrorists – very much aligning with Bush’s Patriot Act. Later, towards the end of the franchise, in 2014, 24: Live Another Day was released. In this series, Bauer was an enemy of the state and federal fugitive. By this point the show felt like it was attempting to reconcile the character’s image with the changing attitudes towards the war crimes of the early 2000s. Whilst 24 remains a relic of that era, the Bond films still continue to regenerate well past the fall of the Soviet Union.

As Pattinson is announced to be the next Bond, protests by workers and students are occurring around the world, from Albania and France to Brazil and the Canada. Giant tech oligarchs are closely working with the government. Data centres continue to be built, and militarism continues to expand. Anarchists hate James Bond, not because we want a foreign government to win, but because we wish for a franchise that disingenuously pretends to value freedom (the concept we champion so dearly) to finally lose.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Trapped in a massive delusion
content:
Notes from the US: The Midterms were an adjustment—voters don’t reject the system, only the system’s products that affect their wallets

The much-anticipated midterm elections produced a significant swing to the Democrats; they now control both houses of Congress – although of course the MAGA/Trump cult is contesting this.

Elation would be inappropriate, though. One of the biggest ‘complaints‘ that voters apparently had about the Republicans was the war against Iran. But because it has raised the price of groceries and petrol and has no aims; not because of the loss of life throughout the Middle East.

Neither during the campaign nor in later public and media analysis was arguably the most important issue facing us discussed: the environment. No candidate stood to make changes. Nor have plans announced by the incoming Democratic party mentioned the environment.

What’s more, although more potentially ‘radical’ congresspersons were elected than ever before, discussion has almost exclusively been about the mechanics of electioneering, party politics, personalities, who will or won’t work with whom ‘across the aisle’. Leaders blethered with furrowed brow and a smile about how it was necessary to look forward not back and not be distracted by the corruption, cruelty, crimes and catastrophes of the Trump/MAGA cult. It’s likely to be probably toothless ‘investigations’, not action.

To be fair, so much damage has been done by Trump so far – DOGE; tariffs; wealth redistribution upward; weaponisation of the law and legal system; health; neutering the media; even the demolition of parts of Washington DC, including the White House, not to mention the environment – that even to go back to the status quo ante would need a massive amount of time, money and energy.

What’s more Trump has already threatened to veto anything he doesn’t like (so really all the aforementioned reversals) and can have his vetoes prevail (the Senate requires 66% votes to overrule presidential vetoes); and his administration has already begun illegally destroying documentation necessary to be preserved as evidence.

Any attempts to oppose Trump in his final two years by ‘investigating’ his crimes in the previous two are also almost certain to be met by simple refusal to comply: they’ll ignore subpoenas; refuse to appear before committees; brush aside court orders etc. If all else fails, they may even get violent. Impeachment seems unlikely.

Credible commentary on the atmosphere and environment in the White House and ‘inner’ government circles reports chaos, in-fighting, backbiting and widespread incompetence as Trump tries to advance an ever more hubristic and absurd agenda. The appointments this week of the combative Jim Jordan as House minority leader, and last week of the ghoulish thug, Stephen Miller, as chief of staff replacing Susie Wiles (who was a touch more professional and efficient) indicate their determination to change nothing. The tone of the fascist propaganda outlets is relentlessly negative, delusional, insulting, inaccurate and alarmist… “The commies have taken over”… and they are going to eat your babies.

None of this is surprising, though. Let’s take a step back and ponder what really motivates these public figures.

When Trump last month suggested naming yet more natural and geographical features after himself (as he has done, particularly across the US capital, Washington DC), he revealed much about the nature of right-wing toxicity.

At a rally in the middle of October he announced that he was considering unilaterally ‘renaming’ the world’s largest ocean after himself. Yes it was perhaps trolling. But he did follow through with Lake Ontario in August. (It’s only a short step from that kind of thing to the way Trump ‘renames’ his opponents in order to try and denigrate them… “I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want”.)

In addition to the off-putting solipsistic, dictatorial and crass nature of these moves they highlight the essence of rightwing, fascist, MAGA, Republican beliefs: me first! Me me me. No-one else matters. It’s almost inconceivable to cult members that anyone else uses, sails across, enjoys the majesty of, has shores on, marvels at or indeed even has a say over under international treaties about the sea.

One might readily assign one of the ‘early’ developmental ages elaborated by Swiss biologist and psychologist Jean Piaget, and with which parents and primary school teachers are familiar to Trump and his kind.

MAGA, Trump, the new far right across the world perversely (but predictably) all make a virtue out of this absorption in Me Me Me… the push to exclude guest-workers, to vilify the LGBTQ+ world, demonise the poor and disabled, to accumulate wealth out of all proportion to whatever could be spent in one super rich oligarch’s lifetime.

Sometimes toxic and harmful self-absorption hits lows that stop you in your tracks – such as when Trump, referring to gubernatorial candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy’s offensive campaign advertisement about his opponent’s abuse as a child, said “I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody.”

Mediaeval theology has something useful to add here: the gravest of the seven deadly sins was pride. It didn’t mean vaunting belongings, parading one’s appearance, having an inflated opinion of oneself. Rather, pride was the sin that it was because its drive to carry through on selfishness. The unadulterated conviction that only one person matters: oneself. Thinkers, poets, philosophers, the clergy and those who acted in what we might now call a therapeutic capacity had a clear idea of how what they saw as self-deception could be confronted and, ideally, avoided. Reflection. Knowledge of oneself. Introspection. Above all: humility. Paradoxically, one could look more closely at one’s behaviour and values specifically to avoid committing the sin.

This, alas, is alien to the powerful minority in such a young and large polity as the United States, which is also isolated geographically. But if the pronouncements of the MAGA cult (and presumably their opponents, who now rule the roost) smacked more of compassion, empathy and selflessness, the enhanced braggadocio leading to institutionalised oppression might perhaps at least be attenuated.

But imagine trying to articulate such a nuanced argument on prime time TV; ‘debate’ in such milieus consists largely of shouting trite counter assertions around the studio.

What’s maybe not obvious, what certainly is not referred to, discussed or analysed in commentary in the US media, is the extent to which cult members do seem actually to believe that their isolationist, selfish, solipsistic elevation of the second Trump presidency to a ‘Golden Age’ in which America really is ‘Great Again’. They really are trapped in a delusion so massive (and so harmful) that there seems to be no shifting them. The recent election represents adjustment within the system. If there is rejection it’s of some of the products of that system which affect voters’ wallets the most, not its innate process.

Last month Trump appointed Katie Zacharia to the post of White House Press Secretary, whose remit is to communicate to and liaise with the press. It didn’t take long for researchers to find out just how inappropriate a person she is for the job… lies, conspiracies, calls for the suspension of habeas corpus, wild accusations against Trump’s opponents, and so on. But they didn’t matter. What did matter in public reaction was that Zacharia had lied about her professional qualifications.

Par for the course, though: at the same time, Trump defied the order from a federal judge to refrain from broadcasting campaign advertisements, which were illegal because they used government money.

If you want a snapshot of how absurd political/public life has become in the US, then look no further than the spectacle of a convicted felon, pathological liar and serial child rapist at its head prancing and lumbering around in a silly little red hat with a fascist slogan as he obsesses on his allies’ buttocks while abolishing the few remaining restraints on fossil fuel emissions as his cult followers like quack ‘health’ secretary, Kennedy spout racist lies, and Texas senator Cruz advocates supremacist murder.

title: Bullshit Burnham’s war on the disabled
content:
Andy Burnham promised an end to forty years of neoliberalism. Instead, he’s embraced the persecution of its favourite scapegoats

The news that the Milburn Review is to recommend the end of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), and the health element of Universal Credit for most young people under the age of 25, is not a surprise to those of us in the disability rights community, but it is horrific all the same.

According to Labour, it’s for their own good; no-one, intones Andy solemnly, wants to be trapped in a cycle of dependency, do they? Of course, this is all bullshit. Intentions matter, and neither the Milburn Review into the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) or the Timms Review into PIP itself, were commissioned for the benefit of the young or the disabled, but for the benefit of the government’s bank balance.

Put simply—and no-one is questioning this—the number of claimants has increased significantly since the pandemic. One million young people are not in work or education. And the government doesn’t want to spend money on the problem.

But the clue is in the chronology. Though COVID has been memory-holed by many, not least government, which has worked assiduously to prevent Long COVID being recognised as a disability, the UK as elsewhere went through a once-in-a-century pandemic a handful of years ago. Apart from the death toll, which the COVID Inquiry acknowledges was worsened by government policy, many were left disabled and chronically ill.

That’s not the whole story, but it’s a big part of it, and as with COVID more generally it’s one government simply pretends doesn’t exist. The Burnham/Milburn rhetoric on disability is one of sympathy, that this is a ‘moral’ choice by government, that these ‘changes’ are an opportunity for a generational reset for young people who have, by Burnham’s own admission, been failed by politicians.

On that last we can agree, but Burnham’s no break with that catalogue of failure. Like his predecessors Starmer and Reeves, Burnham’s characterised PIP as an out-of-work benefit, when it is isn’t – it’s paid to ensure folks can be independent (the clue is in the name) and meet the additional costs which are incurred by being disabled in an ableist society. This is a wilful play into right-wing ‘scrounger’ rhetoric.

Burnham’s not wrong to mention that austerity had an enormous impact on the young in the coalition years, but lest we forget this is a man who lost a previous chance at the Labour leadership primarily because he refused to vote against coalition welfare cuts in 2015, a decision which fuelled a grassroots revolt in the Labour Party and the ultimate election of Jeremy Corbyn.

Indeed, what’s proposed here is a massive real-terms saving to government dressed up as empowerment for its victims—which is the classic Labour play. But anyone with any critical faculty can read Burnham’s words and know they are bullshit.

His constant references to parity of esteem in the education sector could have been written by any government, Labour or Tory, for the last sixty years. As with everything with him, it is surface-level, hoping to play on common-sensical shibboleths that will encourage folks to look past (or not at all at) the actual policy.

The same weekend his op-ed was published, a TikTok found its way online from the Labour account with Andy saying “we used to have a laugh…talk about pub snacks” before the Union Jack came prominently into play. The more things change, the more they stay the same, as the Burnham revolution boils down to idiotic chat about pork scratchings and pints whilst the young have what precious little support they get taken from them.

Labour’s messaging this week is to say that what they propose is more humane than what the Tories want to do, that they are offering a jobs guarantee and hope. But like all Burnham’s promises it’s a mirage. Milburn has proposed a reduction in employer national insurance for young people, but not yet; young people will still be paid less for the same work too.

Young people still won’t be able to access the mental health care they need. They will supposedly be able to apply to ‘local funds’ for support, funds which don’t exist and if they ever did based on prior experience would be unlikely to be responsive. But this rhetoric is just to salve the consciences of those not directly affected.

Disabled people, and disabled young people in particular, are neoliberal capitalism’s favourite scapegoats. In an economic morality which prioritises profit-making productivity over all else, those who find this difficult due to the barriers placed in their way by an ableist society are relentlessly punished.

We disabled people are a cautionary tale, there to remind people to work hard and stay fit else you will join our world of uncertainty and fear. But disability is something which can come to anyone. With that in mind, as anarchists, as socialists, we must emphasise that we are human – not human resources, to be dispensed with once our value is extracted from us.

Kropotkin knew when he promoted mutual aid what was at stake. The fundamental principle of all forms of communism – ‘from each according to their ability, to each according to their need’ must remain our lodestar. As neoliberal politicians seek to strip our dignity with a smile, we must reject their bullshit unequivocally, unapologetically, and in favour of the society we seek to build.

author: Freedom Editor
title: “Britain or Ireland? Neither nation, thanks”
content: Interview: Rave punk provocateurs Them’uns on anti-sectarianism and anti-militarism Them’uns are a rave punk duo from a rural town in north County Antrim (they won’t say which one). On 11 November (Armistice Day), they released a track titled ‘Amarum’, which is Latin for ‘bitter’ – inverting war poet Wilfred Owen’s famous ‘old lie’: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori. But aside from the anti-militarist bangers, but what sort of ‘them’uns’ are Them’uns, exactly? And why is a punk band singing in Latin? We caught up with Jim from the duo to explain… Let’s start with the obvious question: why ‘Them’uns’? Well, there’s a cheeky nod to the old 1960s beat band ‘Them’ from Belfast – though we sound nothing like them, have zero sympathies with Van Morrison’s recent eejitry, and we’re emphatically NOT from Belfast. Then there’s the Norn Irn ‘identity’ bit. In this part of the world, them’uns are the others – we don’t take either side in the ‘two traditions’ carve up, so we’ll always be apart from the mainstream blocs seeking an Irish Union or British Nation (yes, you heard that last bit correctly). You might call us ‘neither-nors’, but not in the limp non-sectarian sense. We’re anti-sectarian anarchists. Is it the ‘anarchist’ provocation that makes you a punk band then, despite all the synthesisers and electronic drum malarkey? Provocation? Yeah, why not? When supposed counter-culturalists allow themselves to be sucked into the mire of nationalism – of any colour – they’re losing any critical edge they might have had. And, look, I know people are hopelessly wedded to their guitar bands, but synthesisers are by far a more democratic instrument. Synths and e-drums are punker than guitars, because anyone really can do it. How’s that for a provocation? And there’s a ton of distortion on everything, if that helps us retain some punk cred. I’m not the arbiter of punk credibility! Let’s get into the new track ‘Amarum’. I can see you’ve lifted some lines from the War poets like Siegfried Sassoon, Charles Hamilton Sorley, and of course Wilfred Owen. But aren’t you losing Owen’s irony by going directly with ‘Bitter and shameful’? (And since when do punk bands sing in Latin, by the way?) The internet killed irony dead! It’s not that people are dumbed-down or too stupid to get it; the online ecosystem is just so full of people arguing in bad faith. They strip away context and nuance, and irony relies entirely on context and nuance, so it’s just become useless nowadays. We have to say it plainly: ‘it’s bitter and shameful to die for your country’. The shame is not on those who die, but on the countries that send them off to be butchered. The bitterness is felt by those staring death in its miserable eye, and by everyone they leave behind. That’s exactly what Owen and the rest of them were saying in the First World War, right? It’s the same meaning with ‘Amarum’, it’s just as anti-militarist, but there’s no room for subtle poesy these days. Amarum by Them’uns This isn’t a pacifist thing, and it’s not a ‘both sides-ism’ thing. But we need to show some anti-militarist spine in the face of aggressively asserted nationalisms – people get swept up in the fervour, alienate ‘other’ humans, and then deadly violence can be excused and even celebrated. You can attach whatever decorous ‘nobility’ you want to that, but we need to ask ourselves: who benefits from our martyrdom? Did you say you were going to send this to Freedom? Maybe we need to do a side mission on Kropotkin? Well, there are a lot of resonances with the build up to the Great War nowadays. But maybe we’ll let him off the hook since he’s been dead for 105 years. Do you think Prince Piotr would have been a rave punk fan? No, Goldman’s the rave punk, for sure. Kropotkin would be into post-hardcore – earnest but with barely concealed mainstream pretensions. Bakunin’s obviously a crusty. Proudhon fronts up a gruff pop punk/orgcore band. Landauer’s an emo. I could go on … So is it true that you’ve got a PhD in Political Philosophy, then? Good to see it being put to good use there Jim. No comment! Speaking of unlikely punk languages, we did do a song in Ulster Scots too. That’s probably more provocative than anything else we’ve said or done, which tells you a lot about the state of ‘cultural warfare’ here in the north of Ireland. Punk Rave EP by Them’uns I was going to ask about that. I’m reminded of another Northern Irish ravey duo, Fun Protestants. You’re both effectively playing up this ‘identity’ angle – is it basically a proddy version of Kneecap? Now you’re the one trying to be provocative! We’ve played with Fun Protestants once before – really dead on people, and I love the music, their album’s great. I can see why you’d point to a similarity, and I’d take it as a compliment. I think what Fun Protestants do is really important, skewering their own cultural background, and maybe in the process pointing to something liberatory and radical that runs through Protestantism in the north of Ireland. But again, I would worry that the ironic critique made by Fun Protestants just gets turned into blatant sectarianism by other people who won’t admit that there’s a progressive element there, or that their own ‘side’ is guilty of similarly regressive small-mindedness. Them’uns takes aim at both sides simultaneously – we have to, because as soon as you pick a side, the game’s over. Like, that’s the opposite of ‘both-sides-ism’, isn’t it? It’s neither-side-ism. You’re reminding me of ‘80s anarcho-punk bands like Toxic Waste with that: ‘Choose and be damned’! Exactly! There were ‘alternative’ bands flirting with nationalism/unionism back then too, of course – That Petrol Emotion and Ruefrex and some other bands spinning off from the punk scene. If it was tragic then, I suppose it must be farcical now. I’ve got a better one for you: ‘If you can’t laugh at yourself, I’ll be happy to do it for you’ – that’s Groucho. Point taken! But I did notice a review in the luminary punk zine MaximumRockNRoll that described Them’uns as ‘British’ – where did that come from? A lazy reviewer! We sent MRR a cassette tape (This is Rave Punk, 2023), but they only ever listened to the Bandcamp page – which had the location set to ‘Antrim, UK’, so the reviewer just decided UK meant Britain, and that therefore we were British. Of course we’re not. We’re from the island of Ireland (but if Ed Sheeran’s ‘Irish’, then we’re not that either, and we’re certainly not going about wearing a tricolour balaclava). But why would you expect a self-satisfied US zine reviewer to understand that sort of geopolitical complexity? He didn’t even listen to the actual tape! There were different versions of the songs on the Bandcamp page – and one song wasn’t on there at all, it was tape-only, so it was obvious that he hadn’t bothered. He didn’t give us a particularly favourable review either (described us as ‘textbook anti-authoritarian’) which might explain why I’m so grumpy about it. Do better next time, Nick Odorizzi! Yes, I feel like you’re bearing a bit of a grudge there, Jim. I thought the first two tapes were a lot of fun, if that’s any consolation. But the new song has a different feel to it. Is that fair to say? Is ‘fun’ a back-handed compliment, Ian? But yeah, that’s fair. We had a line-up change earlier this year. Amy’s come in and plays some lead synth, which we didn’t have before. The e-drum set up has been stripped back to just two pads. And we recorded this one ourselves, so maybe it’s a bit more raw but more musically expansive? We pretend to make a punk virtue out of capturing all the sounds live, rather than relying on production tricks – but honestly we were just worried that we’d screw it up because we’re not that clever at using Digital Audio Workstation software. We spent time getting the right sounds to come out of the synths and amps and microphones, and then just mixed that – there’s not even any equalisation on it! I’m willing to award some bonus punk points for that. So, give us the plug then – how can people hear it? ‘Amarum’ is coming out as a digital thing with Do It With Others Records, and all their proceeds go directly to anarchist causes. DIWO do everything as ‘pay what you want’ – kudos to Marko! Two more tracks from that recording session are coming out as a DIY 7” vinyl release on 11th December, titled ‘Ballymetropolis’/‘Mouth Ulster’ – we’re playing a gig locally in Coleraine to launch that one. There’s a streamable version on Bandcamp, and you can pre-order the physical record there too. title: A day of general strike in Spain
content:
A chronicle of pre-dawn picket lines, massive demonstrations, persistent rain, and sharply differing figures on participation

The strike began before dawn. By midnight, the first picket lines were already being organized. In Valencia, the CGT union had called for pickets at the Mercavalència wholesale market starting at 2:00 a.m., and at the EMT (municipal transport) depots in San Isidro from 5:00 a.m. Subsequently, access routes into the city—including the V-21 highway and the Ronda Nord—were blocked. The coverage in Valencia tracked the movement from the wholesale markets to the municipal transport network.

In Catalonia, actions were concentrated from the early hours at the Mercabarna wholesale market, various workplaces, and along roadways. According to updates published throughout the morning, more than thirty locations across the road network were affected by blockades. In Madrid, “informational” picket lines gathered at the EMT transport depots in Fuencarral and Carabanchel; the CCOO and UGT unions reported police charges and the use of pepper spray against participants.

At the Mercamadrid wholesale market, unions also reported police intervention. Reports concerning the Madrid transport depots include statements from the organisations involved. Tension spread to Málaga, where reports emerged of police charges near the EMT (municipal transport company) depots, and to Zamora, where early reports indicated two arrests and four people requiring emergency medical attention following an incident involving a transport picket line. In the Basque Country, the Ertzaintza (Basque police) reported thirteen arrests as of mid-morning, eight of which took place in Portugalete. These were preliminary tallies from different regions and points in time.

Initial reports from labour unions indicated high participation in certain industrial sectors. CCOO and UGT estimated that 90% of workers in the automotive and port sectors, and 85% in the meat-processing industry, participated during the early shifts. The CGT also reported high levels of work stoppages and picket activity. These estimates come from the organisations themselves, refer to specific sectors and shifts, and do not, on their own, confirm the overall percentage of workers on strike. The initial industrial report provides further detail on its source.

In the Valencian Community, the figures varied significantly. UGT-PV reported over 70% participation in industrial firms with union representation, while the employers’ association, CEV, estimated a 2.57% participation rate across the region’s entire economic sector during the early hours. Later, CCOO and UGT reported an average participation rate of 60% in the region. These figures are not directly comparable, as they differ in scope, the population observed, and the timeframes considered. Examining both sets of figures helps to explain these discrepancies.

The strike also affected public media. Canal Sur Televisión interrupted its regular programming around 8:20 a.m. while the show Despierta Andalucía was airing. In Valencia, nearly fifty students staged a sit-in at the Faculty of Geography and History at the University of Valencia in support of the strike. Picket groups focused on commercial areas moved through the streets and neighbourhoods of various cities. In the Vila de Gràcia neighbourhood, the mobilisation coincided with the postponement of an eviction.

The struggle for housing did not emerge as an issue separate from working conditions. Tenants’ unions, labour unions, and neighbourhood assemblies brought demands against high rents to the picket lines, alongside the defence of wages, public services, and labour rights. In Bilbao, groups converged in front of the Arriaga Theatre before heading toward the Basque Government headquarters. In Pamplona (Iruñea), a protest in front of CaixaBank ended with one arrest, according to reports on the day’s events. In Barcelona, ​​a main picket line moved through the commercial district; in Madrid, there were blockades on the Gran Vía and the Carrera de San Jerónimo.

By the afternoon, the strike had reached the major avenues.

Barcelona saw one of the largest marches. Groups arriving from various neighborhoods converged at the Jardinets and the Passeig de Gràcia. The Tenants’ Union (Sindicat de Llogateres) estimated the turnout at 400,000 people, while the local police (Guardia Urbana) provided an estimate of 55,000. These figures come from different sources, with no independent assessment to resolve the discrepancy. After the march concluded, La Directa and El Salto reported that the Mossos (Catalan police) had carried out charges in the city centre.

In Valencia, a unified demonstration took place in the rain. The march moved along Calle Colón and reached the Plaza del Ayuntamiento, with participation from labour unions and housing advocacy groups. El Salto reported tens of thousands of participants, while other media outlets described thousands of attendees and a historic demonstration. The live coverage by Sindicalismo.org could not verify an exact figure provided by the organisers; therefore, that description is not translated here into a specific number. Levante-EMV and Europa Press published accounts of the march.

In Zaragoza, the National Police estimated 20,000 protesters, while the organisers claimed 60,000. In Lleida, the Guardia Urbana (local police) estimated 4,500 attendees, compared to 14,000 according to the unions. In Granada, El Salto reported two separate marches, estimating at least 8,000 people in each. Girona and Manresa also saw large-scale demonstrations, according to the organising groups. In Madrid, the march from Atocha toward Plaza de España proceeded through the rain, with housing issues serving as one of its central demands.

Severe weather impacted the day’s events in Andalusia. CCOO and UGT canceled their afternoon demonstrations in Cádiz, Huelva, Córdoba, and Seville as conditions worsened. However, a separate mobilisation took place in Seville, organised by housing groups and organisations such as the CGT, CNT, and USTEA. The cancellation of one event did not mean that all protests in the city were called off.

Reports of police charges and the identification of individuals emerged alongside the strike, beginning with the very first picket lines. In Granada, the Andalusian Association for Human Rights (Asociación Pro Derechos Humanos de Andalucía) called for an investigation into police interventions near the Metro and the Alhambra, reporting a rib injury and difficulties in identifying the officers involved. In Madrid, El Salto reported the use of pepper spray and rubber bullets during an intervention that took place after the demonstration had concluded, in the area of ​​Plaza de España. In Tarragona, Alerta Solidària reported that individuals were injured by foam projectiles during a protest near the Palau de Congressos. These are reported incidents and allegations attributed to specific sources, not judicial findings.

The tally of arrests published by Sindicalismo.org recorded 52 detainees and 919 incidents as of 5:00 PM, based on data available at that time from the Ministry of the Interior and regional police forces: 38 arrests by the National Police and Civil Guard, 13 reported by the Ertzaintza, and one by the Mossos. This figure superseded previous counts of 40 and 42 arrests; these numbers should not be added together.

The figures shifted later that evening: at 9:45 PM, the Mossos reported 18 arrests in the centre of Barcelona—a local figure that emerged after the 5:00 PM national tally. This cannot simply be added to the 52 without first verifying potential overlaps or the timing of the events. Trade unions and anti-repression organisations demanded explanations and defended the right to strike, while police forces justified their interventions by citing incidents they attributed to protesters. A final, definitive figure for the entire day was not available from the sources consulted for this report.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Dignity walks in the heart
content:
Mexico’s search collectives make alliances with Zapatista army to confront the systematic violence of enforced disappearances and femicides

It is dawn again and 12-year-old Ariana is getting ready to leave her home with her grandmother. Together they walk in the mountains of Chiapas to a nearby ranch to care for their family animals. After that? We cannot say, as they both stepped out of this world and disappeared. We only know for sure that they were never seen alive again.

The family and neighbours began the search until two days later, the body of 55-year-old Miriam Cruz Alpuche was discovered on the bank of a local stream. She was wrapped in black bin bags and community rescue units discovered multiple signs of violence. By the end of the week, Ariana Scarlet Velázquez Cruz was found close by.

“The demand for truth and justice for disappearances,” said Captain Marcos of the EZLN (Zapatista Army of National Liberation) “enforced disappearances and disappearances by individuals – must be assumed a national responsibility.” Marcos was speaking in San Cristóbal de las Casas (Jovel) in Chiapas after meeting with “mother seekers” in el caracol Jacinto Canel.

In the Zapatista territories, EZLN and colectivos de búsqueda (search collectives) have pledged to form alliances in confronting the Mexican government for it’s role in facilitating disappearances, murders, gender-based violence and wars. They will meet in Ajusco in December, an area that is a high risk for disappearances, as well as a delegation to Mexico City to both expose and find community-based resistance to this crime against humanity.

With more than 130,000 people missing in Mexico, decades of activism and legal battles against systematic violence and enforced disappearances, the United Nations has finally got involved in offering the state of Mexico assistance. Predictably as the families of the disappeared arrived to give their own testimony, the Mexican government denied this pain with their own historical fiction.

In Chiapas there have been 30 documented cases of femicide and 440 across Mexico in the first half of 2026. These numbers are reflections of the activities of local groups, not the true scale of the problem. Government corruption has hidden the mass killings of women and children, as well as a clear complicity in the enforced disappearances of it’s own citizens. If the body is never recovered, it cannot be known how the person died.

Investigations into femicides in Mexico are impacted by a loss of evidence, an inadequate investigation or when the gender perspective is not applied correctly. Families of the missing are re-victimised by the process of seeking justice while authorities fail to examine crime scenes, secure evidence or carry out acid phosphatase tests. All of this impacts the possibility of justice for the affected and their families.

Femicidal violence “leaves indelible consequences, deep traumas and an irreparable void in their families… in their communities and in the entire social fabric of the state,” said the Observatorio Ciudadano Nacional del Feminicidio (National Citizen Observatory of Femicide) following the murder of Miriam and Ariana. They demand an immediate gender – child perspective investigation.

The inaction of the authorities when a woman or child has gone missing is deadly, with some regional police asking families to wait 72 hours before reporting a missing person. This would have been too late for Miriam, as it would likely be for 12-year-old Ariana. The logic should be to investigate when a person is noticed missing.

In the absence of executing justice, various instruments of the law such as the Attorney General’s Office (FGE) work as a mechanism to prevent the opening of investigations, with “omission… a lack of commitment and responsibility,” observed Guadalupe Isabel Mondoza Pérez, who has been looking for her husband Alfonso since July 30, 2024 after he disappeared in Yajalón.

Authorities limit complaints by creating an administrative hole called “registros de attención” (care records) as a way of killing formal investigations. With legal advice from Colectiva Cereza (Cherry Collective), families can see what missing persons reports have been shelved in care records and which are open investigations.

If the aim is to tear the social fabric of our shared relations – it would make sense to weave these communities with shared struggles and resources to resist the stranglehold of the law as systematic violence. It is a rebellion to demand social responsibility from top to bottom and reach out to those who seek justice for their loved ones; dead, alive or caught in between.

What unites all activists in the various regional search collectives is a rejection of the government’s narrative of the decline of disappearances and token offerings of dedicated government departments that seemingly do nothing to combat the 40 disappearances a day or provide effective prevention strategies to address the problem.

María Tequi, founder of the Guerreras Buscadoras de Guaymas collective denounced the government’s strategy of making the disappearances in Chiapas invisible by claiming that the reasons why young men are missing are because they migrated to get a job. This narrative is powerful on both southern and northern borders, claiming that people are missing because they left “to work out of necessity.”

“They keep disappearing, they keep killing us. The missing are not absent” María says, “our disappeared are missing because the were taken away, they are not absent of their own free will.” María continues to search for her son Fernando who disappeared in August 2015.

Speaking to the United Nations, Cristina Bautista explained how she will continue to demand justice for her son Benjamin, who on the night of the September 26, 2014 was disappeared with 43 other students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers’ College by the local, state and federal police, in collusion with criminal organisations and the military.

“If we, as fathers and mothers of the 43 students of Ayotzinapa do not shut up, it is so that it does not continue to happen to the other parents, to the other students, that they do not continue to disappear because it is a very great suffering.” By sunrise on September 27; six people were dead, forty wounded and 43 missing. Most of these enforced disappearances have never been found.

The government investigated itself and the Attorney General’s Office came up with it’s own narrative of events calling it “historical truth.” Yet the findings of Forensic Architecture and local civil society collectives discovered a constructed, fraudulent and inconsistent narrative. This fiction protects the impunity of the Mexican state, as it’s governments play both policeman and murderer in a play where half of the cast are missing from the stage.

Almost three decades ago we remember the 1997 massacre in Acteal, where 100 paramilitary soldiers entered a church and murdered 45 people who had taken refuge there. The victims were mostly woman and children and all were members of Las Abejas (The Bees), a libertarian pacifist group who were politically sympathetic to the EZLN. The local police and military refused to intervene as the massacre went on for hours.

The Mexican government denied involvement but leaked plans for a counter-insurgency in Chiapas disproved this assertion, as does the fact that the old paramilitary structures of the 1990 remain intact, with some of the perpetrators of the massacres continuing raids. When tyranny is law, horizontal solidarity with groups and resources is our only way to challenge this form of systematic violence.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum believes the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances (CED) is over-reaching it’s mandate because there is ‘progress’ in the search for missing persons and the government is in ‘dialogue’ with the families of the missing. Enforced disappearance is a crime against humanity, even if committed by individuals under consent of state actors.

“We are concerned,” said Elizabeth Uruchurtu at the UN, “that in order to please it’s political allies, an image of a state that imparts justice is presented when it does not correspond to the reality we live. Enforced disappearance not only disappears people, it also tries to disappear truth, destroy evidence, sow fear and guarantee impunity.”

Daniela González has been looking for her 16-year-old son Axel since June 23, 2022 when he disappeared. Like many, Daniela had to organise to get justice for her son and is now a member of the search collective Una Luz en el Camino.

“The truth is that we have long sought this meeting, this dialogue with the Zapatista army,” Daniela said. “Fortunately today it is achieved and not only is dialogue but it is to be able to weave community, be able to knit and embrace to continue looking for our loved ones.”

“We recognize their struggle,” families of the missing wrote before the meeting, “and the exercise of autonomy and resistance to power, as well as the search for ways to a dignified life.”

author: Freedom Editor
title: A regressive love-letter to traditional journalism
content:
Film review: The Social Reckoning is both deeply attached to the liberal United States and terrified of what it has become

When history is written, how will the last 30 years be remembered? If The Social Reckoning is anything to go by, it will be as a slow slide into a paranoid dystopia. This film presents the most depressing view of the contemporary United States that I have seen to date, and that it does so from the heart of the Hollywood mainstream only makes this more striking. This is a shamelessly conservative romance that idealises middle-class, liberal and sexist American values in contrast to today’s proto-fascist, hyper-capitalist hellscape.

Frances Haugan, whose ethical compass is the film’s North star, is in a codependent relationship with her company. She loves Facebook, but when she stumbles on evidence of its corrupting influence, she is unable to raise the problem internally, and expects to be caught and punished for blowing the whistle. Like a late-period Stasi spy, she quickly comes to distrust her superiors, her society, and the other side, while remaining attached to a myth of instant, universal connection.

In the USSR, that myth was of communism as an approaching, abundant and benevolent equality. Here, Frances’s utopia is a world without “human friction”, where everyone communicates and everyone gets along. The spanner in the works is the profit motive.
